nodes.name: Fix arguments and gamma
nodes.statement:
Let $X_i \in \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{H}) \cap \mathcal{S}^{\alpha_i}(\mathcal{H}), 1 \leq i \leq n-1$, and let $Y$ be a finite-rank operator on $\mathcal{H}$ such that $\|Y\|_{\alpha'} \leq 1$. Let
$$\gamma := \liminf_k \| \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi_k)\|_{\mathcal{B}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}^{\alpha_1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{S}^{\alpha_{n-1}}, \mathcal{S}^{\alpha})}.$$
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Fix $X_i$, a finite-rank $Y$, and let $\gamma$ be the liminf of the norms.

nodes.name: Duality bound
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Bound the trace pairing with $Y$ by $\gamma\prod\|X_i\|$ using $w^*$-continuity, giving (3).

nodes.name: Norm bound
nodes.statement:
This implies that $\Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi) \in \mathcal{B}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}^{\alpha_1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{S}^{\alpha_{n-1}}, \mathcal{S}^{\alpha})$ with
$$
\| \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi)\|_{\mathcal{B}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}^{\alpha_1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{S}^{\alpha_{n-1}}, \mathcal{S}^{\alpha})} \leq \gamma.
$$
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Conclude boundedness of $\Gamma(\varphi)$ with norm at most $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Approximants
nodes.statement:
Let $0 < \epsilon < 1$. For any $1 \leq i \leq n-1$, let $X_i \in \mathcal{S}^{\alpha_i}(\mathcal{H}), \tilde{X}_i \in \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{H}) \cap \mathcal{S}^{\alpha_i}(\mathcal{H})$ such that $\| X_i - \tilde{X}_i \|_{\alpha_i} \leq \epsilon$. Let $Z \in \mathcal{S}^{\alpha'}(\mathcal{H})$ and $Y$ be a finite-rank operator on $\mathcal{H}$ such that $\| Z - Y \|_{\alpha'} \leq \epsilon$. Write, for any $k\geq 1$,
$$\Gamma_{k,X} = \left[\Gamma^{A_1,A_2, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi_k)\right](X_1,\ldots, X_{n-1})$$
and
$$\tilde{\Gamma}_{k,X} = \left[\Gamma^{A_1,A_2, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi_k)\right](\tilde{X}_1, \ldots, \tilde{X}_{n-1}).
$$
Similarly, write
$$\Gamma_{X} = \left[\Gamma^{A_1,A_2, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi)\right](X_1,\ldots,X_{n-1})$$
and
$$\tilde{\Gamma}_X = \left[\Gamma^{A_1,A_2, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi)\right](\tilde{X}_1, \ldots, \tilde{X}_{n-1}).
$$
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Introduce approximations $\tilde X_i\in\mathcal{S}^2$ and finite-rank $Y$, and notation $\Gamma_{k,X}$, $\tilde\Gamma_{k,X}$.

nodes.name: Uniform error from Remark 2.2
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Apply Remark 2.2 to bound the approximation errors uniformly in $k$.

nodes.name: Convergence on approximants
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: On approximants the trace pairings converge.

nodes.name: Five-term estimate
nodes.statement:
Hence, by \eqref{Proofineqp}, \eqref{lemma1simp} and \eqref{lemma2simp} we have, for any $k\geq k_0$,
\begin{align*}
& | {\mathrm{Tr}\,}(\Gamma_{X}Z) - {\mathrm{Tr}\,}(\Gamma_{k,X}Z) | \\
& \leq | {\mathrm{Tr}\,}(\Gamma_{X}(Z-Y)) | + | {\mathrm{Tr}\,}((\Gamma_{X} - \tilde{\Gamma}_{X})Y) | + | {\mathrm{Tr}\,}((\tilde{\Gamma}_{X} - \tilde{\Gamma}_{k,X})Y) | \\
& \ \ \ + | {\mathrm{Tr}\,}((\tilde{\Gamma}_{k,X} - \Gamma_{k,X})Y) | + | {\mathrm{Tr}\,}(\Gamma_{k,X}(Y-Z)) | \\
& \leq \left(\gamma \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \|X_i\|_{\alpha_i} + C \|Y\|_{\alpha'} + 1 + C \|Y\|_{\alpha'} + C'\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \|X_i\|_{\alpha_i} \right) \epsilon.
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality bounds the pairing difference by a constant times $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Weak convergence
nodes.statement:
Since $\|Y\|_{\alpha'} \leq \|Z\|_{\alpha'} + \epsilon$, we proved that $$
\left[ \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi_k) \right](X_1, \ldots, X_{n-1}) \underset{k \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \left[ \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\varphi) \right](X_1, \ldots, X_{n-1})
$$
weakly in $\mathcal{S}^{\alpha}(\mathcal{H})$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Conclude weak convergence in $\mathcal{S}^\alpha$.

nodes.name: Case p=2, elementary tensors
nodes.statement:
Assume that $p=2$. We first prove the result when $\phi_1 = f_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes f_n$ and $\phi_2 = g_j \otimes g_{j+1}$ where for any $1\leq i \leq n, f_i\in L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_i}), g_j \in L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_j}), g_{j+1} \in L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_{j+1}})$. In this case,
$$
\phi_1 \widetilde{\phi_2} = f_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes f_{j-1} \otimes f_j g_j \otimes f_{j+1} g_{j+1} \otimes f_{j+2} \otimes \cdots \otimes f_n
$$
so we have, by \eqref{MOItensor},
\begin{align*}
& \left[ \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\phi_1 \widetilde{\phi_2})\right] (K_1, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = f_1(A_1)K_1 \ldots K_{j-1} f_j(A_j) g_j(A_j) K_j g_{j+1}(A_{j+1}) f_{j+1}(A_{j+1}) K_{j+1} \ldots K_{n-1}f_n(A_n) \\
& = f_1(A_1)K_1 \ldots K_{j-1} f_j(A_j) \left[\Gamma^{A_j, A_{j+1}}(g_j\otimes g_{j+1})\right](K_j) f_{j+1}(A_{j+1}) K_{j+1} \ldots K_{n-1}f_n(A_n) \\
& = \left[ \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\phi_1)\right] \left(K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, \left[\Gamma^{A_j, A_{j+1}}(\phi_2)\right](K_j), K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}\right),
\end{align*}
which proves the result for such $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: For $p=2$ and elementary tensors, compute directly from (2).

nodes.name: Extend by bilinearity
nodes.statement: Note that this formula is bilinear in $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$, hence the result holds true whenever $\phi_1 \in L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1}) \otimes \cdots \otimes L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_n})$ and $\phi_2 \in L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_j}) \otimes L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_{j+1}})$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Extend to algebraic tensors by bilinearity.

nodes.name: Approximating nets
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $\phi_1,\phi_2$ by nets of tensors; the formula holds for each pair, (8).

nodes.name: Limit of right-hand side
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: $w^*$-continuity gives the limit of the right-hand side of (8).

nodes.name: w*-convergence of products
nodes.statement:
For the left-hand side of \eqref{for1}, we show that $(\phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_{2,t}})_{t\in T}$ $w^*$-converges to $\phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_2}$. Indeed, let $g\in L^1(\lambda_{A_1} \times \cdots \times \lambda_{A_n})$. Then, writing $\Omega = \sigma(A_1) \times \cdots \times \sigma(A_n)$, we have, by Fubini's theorem,
\begin{align*}
& \int_{\Omega} \phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_{2,t}} ~ g \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_1} \cdots \text{d}\lambda_{A_n} \\
& = \int_{\sigma(A_j) \times \sigma(A_{j+1})} \phi_{2,t} \left( \int_{\prod_{i \neq j,j+1} \sigma(A_i)} \phi_{1,s} g \ \prod_{i \neq j,j+1}\text{d}\lambda_{A_j} \right) \text{d}\lambda_{A_j}\text{d}\lambda_{A_{j+1}} \\
& := \int_{\sigma(A_j) \times \sigma(A_{j+1})} \phi_{2,t} \psi_s \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_j}\text{d}\lambda_{A_{j+1}}.
\end{align*}
By Fubini's theorem, we have the inequality
\begin{align*}
\int_{\sigma(A_j) \times \sigma(A_{j+1})} | \psi_s | \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_j}\text{d}\lambda_{A_{j+1}}
& \leq \int_{\Omega} | \phi_{1,s} g | \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_1} \cdots \text{d}\lambda_{A_n} \\
& \leq \| \phi_{1,s} \|_{\infty} \| g\|_{1},
\end{align*}
which shows that $\psi_s \in L^1(\lambda_{A_j} \times \lambda_{A_{j+1}})$. Hence,
$$
\int_{\sigma(A_j) \times \sigma(A_{j+1})} \phi_{2,t} \psi_s \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_j}\text{d}\lambda_{A_{j+1}} \underset{t}{\longrightarrow} \int_{\sigma(A_j) \times \sigma(A_{j+1})} \phi_2 \psi_s \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_j}\text{d}\lambda_{A_{j+1}},
$$
which is in turn equal to $\displaystyle \int_{\Omega} \phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_2} ~ g \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_1} \cdots \text{d}\lambda_{A_n}$. This shows that $(\phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_{2,t}})_{t\in T}$ $w^*$-converges to $\phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_2}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Show $\phi_{1,s}\widetilde{\phi_{2,t}}\to\phi_{1,s}\widetilde{\phi_2}$ weak-*.

nodes.name: Fubini rewriting
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the pairing with Fubini as an integral of $\phi_{2,t}\psi_s$.

nodes.name: psi_s integrable
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Show $\psi_s\in L^1$.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement:
Hence,
$$
\int_{\sigma(A_j) \times \sigma(A_{j+1})} \phi_{2,t} \psi_s \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_j}\text{d}\lambda_{A_{j+1}} \underset{t}{\longrightarrow} \int_{\sigma(A_j) \times \sigma(A_{j+1})} \phi_2 \psi_s \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_j}\text{d}\lambda_{A_{j+1}},
$$
which is in turn equal to $\displaystyle \int_{\Omega} \phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_2} ~ g \ \text{d}\lambda_{A_1} \cdots \text{d}\lambda_{A_n}$. This shows that $(\phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_{2,t}})_{t\in T}$ $w^*$-converges to $\phi_{1,s} \widetilde{\phi_2}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Weak-* convergence of $\phi_{2,t}$ gives the claim.

nodes.name: Limit in t
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Take the limit in $t$ to get (9).

nodes.name: Limit in s
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Extend by linearity and take the limit in $s$: the identity for $p=2$.

nodes.name: Case general p: bound
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: For general $p$ and $K_i\in\mathcal{S}^2\cap\mathcal{S}^p$, bound the right-hand side, (10).

nodes.name: Bound left-hand side
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Equality (7) transfers the bound to the left-hand side, (11).

nodes.name: Boundedness by density
nodes.statement: By density of $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{H}) \cap \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, we get that $\Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_n}(\phi_1 \widetilde{\phi_2}) \in \mathcal{B}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))$ and that inequalities \eqref{densitysimp1} and \eqref{densitysimp2} hold true for any $K_1, \ldots, K_{n-1} \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Density gives $\Gamma(\phi_1\widetilde{\phi_2})\in\mathcal{B}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}^p)$.

nodes.name: Equality by approximation
nodes.statement: Finally, to prove equality \eqref{fortildeeq} in the case when $K_1, \ldots, K_{n-1} \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, we approximate $K_i, 1\leq i \leq n-1,$ by elements of $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{H}) \cap \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, using inequalities \eqref{densitysimp1} and \eqref{densitysimp2}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $K_i$ to get (7) on $\mathcal{S}^p$.

nodes.name: Case p=2, tensors
nodes.statement: Assume first that $p=2$. In the case when $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are elementary tensors, it is straightforward to check the identity \eqref{simplificationsepid}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: For $p=2$ the identity is immediate on elementary tensors.

nodes.name: Approximating nets
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Approximate by nets of tensors, giving (13).

nodes.name: Iterated limits
nodes.statement: For a fixed $s\in S$, $(\phi_{1,s} \phi_{2,t})_{t\in T}$ converges to $\phi_{1,s} \phi_2$ and $(\phi_{1,s} \phi_2)_{s\in S}$ converges to $\phi = \phi_1 \phi_2$ for the $w^*$-topology of $L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1} \times \cdots \times \lambda_{A_n})$. Hence by taking the limit on $t\in T$ and then on $s\in S$ in \eqref{simplificationsepid2}, we get \eqref{simplificationsepid}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Take iterated $w^*$-limits in $t$ then $s$ to get (12).

nodes.name: Boundedness for general p
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Bound the product of the two MOIs to get boundedness on $\mathcal{S}^p$.

nodes.name: Equality by approximation
nodes.statement: Finally, we deduce \eqref{simplificationsepid} by approximation like in the proof of Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Density argument as in Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: Reduction to (i)
nodes.statement: We only prove $(i)$, in the case when $n\geq 3$. The case $n=2$ and the second and third claims can be proved similarly.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Only case (i) with $n\ge3$ is proved; the others are similar.

nodes.name: Elementary tensors
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: For $p=2$ and elementary tensors, compute directly.

nodes.name: Extend by linearity
nodes.statement: By linearity, this formula holds true whenever $\phi \in L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1}) \otimes \cdots L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_{j-1}}) \otimes L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_{j+1}}) \otimes \cdots \otimes L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_n})$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Extend to algebraic tensors.

nodes.name: Weak-* approximation
nodes.statement: In the general case, we let $(\phi_s)_{s\in S} \subset L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1}) \otimes \cdots L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_{j-1}}) \otimes L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_{j+1}}) \otimes \cdots \otimes L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_n})$ to be a net converging to $\phi$ for the $w^*$-topology of $L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1} \times \cdots \times \lambda_{A_{j-1}} \times \lambda_{A_{j+1}} \times \cdots \times \lambda_{A_n})$. For any $s\in S$, we define $\widetilde{\phi_s}$ as in \eqref{fortilde2}. Then, it is easy to see that $(\widetilde{\phi_s})_{s\in S}$ converges to $\widetilde{\phi}$ for the $w^*$-topology of $L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1} \times \cdots \times \lambda_{A_n})$. We conclude using the $w^*$-continuity of multiple operator integral like in the proof of Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: Approximate by nets and use $w^*$-continuity as in Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: General p
nodes.statement: In the case when $1\leq p < \infty$, we argue as in the end of the proof of Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$. Details are left to the reader.
nodes.section: 2.1 Multiple operator integrals associated to selfadjoint operators
nodes.statement_short: General $p$ by the density argument of Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: Difference quotients g_k
nodes.statement: Define, for any $k\geq 1$, $g_k(t) = k (f^{(n-1)}(t+1/k) - f^{(n-1)}(t)), t\in \mathbb{R}$. Then $(g_k)_{k\geq 1} \subset C(\mathbb{R})$ is pointwise convergent to $f^{(n)}$ and we have the inequality $|g_k| \leq \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $f^{(n)}$ by continuous difference quotients $g_k$ bounded by $\|f^{(n)}\|_\infty$.

nodes.name: Potapov-Skripka-Sukochev bound
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 5.3]{PSS-SSF}, there exists a constant $c_{p,n} > 0$ depending only on $p$ and $n$ such that, for any $k\geq 1$,
\begin{align} \| \Gamma^{A_1,A_2, \ldots, A_{n+1}}(\varphi_{n,g_k}) \|_{\mathcal{B}_n(\mathcal{S}^{pn} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{S}^{pn},\mathcal{S}^p)} \leq c_{p,n} \|g_k \|_{\infty} \leq c_{p,n} \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}.
\end{align}
The proof is given in the case when $A_1 = \cdots = A_{n+1}$ but the arguments from the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.2]{LMS} allow to extend the result in the case when $A_1, \ldots, A_{n+1}$ are distinct.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the uniform bound for $\Gamma(\varphi_{n,g_k})$, (18), extended to distinct $A_i$.

nodes.name: Pointwise convergence
nodes.statement:
By Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem, $\varphi_{n,g_k}$ is pointwise convergent to $\varphi_{n,f^{(n)}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Moreover, we have
$$
|\varphi_{n,g_k}| \leq \dfrac{\|g_k\|_{\infty}}{n!} \leq \dfrac{\|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}}{n!}.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Dominated convergence: $\varphi_{n,g_k}\to\varphi_{n,f^{(n)}}$ pointwise with a uniform bound.

nodes.name: Weak-* convergence
nodes.statement: Hence, using Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem again, we get that $(\varphi_{n,g_k})_{k\geq 1}$ $w^*$-converges to $\varphi_{n,f^{(n)}} = f^{[n]}$ for the $w^*$-topology of $L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1} \times \cdots \times \lambda_{A_{n+1}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\varphi_{n,g_k}\to f^{[n]}$ weak-*.

nodes.name: Conclude via Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement:
By Lemma $\ref{LemmeUB}$ and \eqref{Approxder} we deduce that
$$
\Gamma^{A_1,A_2, \ldots, A_{n+1}}(f^{[n]}) \in \mathcal{B}_n(\mathcal{S}^{pn} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{S}^{pn},\mathcal{S}^p)
$$
with $\| \Gamma^{A_1,A_2, \ldots, A_{n+1}}(f^{[n]}) \|_{\mathcal{B}_n(\mathcal{S}^{pn} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{S}^{pn},\mathcal{S}^p)} \leq c_{p,n} \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}$, from which we deduce inequality \eqref{IneqDDn}. Inequality \eqref{IneqDDn2} follows from the fact that $\|.\|_{pn} \leq \|.\|_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.3 gives the bound (16), and (17) follows.

nodes.name: Divided difference identity
nodes.statement_short: Note the identity (19) from the symmetry of divided differences.

nodes.name: Cut-off symbols
nodes.statement:
Let $k\geq 1$. Define $\phi_1 = f^{[n]}$, and for any $(x_0, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$,
$$
\phi_2(x_{j-1},x_j) = (x_{j-1} - x_j)\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j-1})\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j}),
$$
$$\psi_1(x_0, \ldots, x_n) = f^{[n-1]}(x_0,\ldots,x_{j-1}, x_{j+1}, \ldots,x_n)\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j-1})\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j})$$ and
$$\psi_2(x_0, \ldots, x_n) = f^{[n-1]}(x_0,\ldots,x_{j-2}, x_{j},x_{j+1},\ldots,x_n)\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j-1})\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Define cut-off symbols $\phi_1,\phi_2,\psi_1,\psi_2$.

nodes.name: Functional identity
nodes.statement:
Then $\phi_1, \psi_1, \psi_2 \in L^{\infty}(\lambda_{A_1} \times \cdots \times  \lambda_{A_{j-1}} \times \lambda_B \times \lambda_A \times \lambda_{A_j} \times \cdots \times \lambda_{A_n})$, $\phi_2 \in L^{\infty}(\lambda_B \times \lambda_A)$ and after multiplying equality \eqref{eqDDsep} by $\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j-1})\chi_{[-k,k]}(x_{j})$ we obtain
\begin{equation} \phi_1 \widetilde{\phi_2} = \psi_1 - \psi_2,
\end{equation}
where $\widetilde{\phi_2}$ was defined in \eqref{fortilde}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying (19) by cut-offs gives $\phi_1\widetilde{\phi_2}=\psi_1-\psi_2$, (20).

nodes.name: Case 2<=j<=n-1
nodes.statement:
Assume first that $2 \leq j \leq n-1$. Let $X, K_1, \ldots, K_{n-1} \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$. Note that
$$
\left[\Gamma^{B,A}(\chi_{[-k,-k]} \otimes \chi_{[-k,-k]})\right](X) = p_k(B)Xp_k(A)
$$
and
$$
\left[\Gamma^{B,A}(\phi_2)\right](X) = Bp_k(B)Xp_k(A) - p_k(B)Xp_k(A)A,
$$
where $p_k = \chi_{[-k,k]}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $2\le j\le n-1$: compute $\Gamma^{B,A}$ of the cut-off symbols.

nodes.name: Shorthand
nodes.statement:
Denote
$$\Gamma_A = \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_{j-1}, A, A_j, \ldots, A_{n-1}}, \ \Gamma_B = \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_{j-1}, B, A_j, \ldots, A_{n-1}}$$
and
$$\Gamma_{B,A} = \Gamma^{A_1, \ldots, A_{j-1}, B, A, A_j, \ldots, A_{n-1}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\Gamma_A,\Gamma_B,\Gamma_{B,A}$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemmas 2.4 and 2.6
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\Gamma_{B,A}$ to (20) using Lemmas 2.4 and 2.6, giving (21).

nodes.name: Substitute X = P_i
nodes.statement_short: Take quasi-commuting projections $P_i$ and set $X=P_i$, giving (23).

nodes.name: Limit of right-hand side
nodes.statement_short: Right-hand side converges by continuity from Theorem 2.7.

nodes.name: Limit of left-hand side
nodes.statement:
Using the identity
$$
Bp_k(B)P_ip_k(A) - p_k(B)P_ip_k(A)A = p_k(B)(BP_i-P_iB)p_k(A) + p_k(B)P_i(B-A)p_k(A),
$$
we have, by \eqref{existpro}, that
$$
Bp_k(B)P_ip_k(A) - p_k(B)P_ip_k(A)A \to p_k(B)(B-A)p_k(A)
$$
in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, as $i$ goes to $\infty$. Hence, the left-hand side of \eqref{eqfunc3} converges in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ to
$$
\left[ \Gamma_{B,A}(f^{[n]})\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, p_k(B)(B-A)p_k(A), K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})
$$
and we proved that
\begin{align} \begin{split}
& \left[ \Gamma_{B,A}(f^{[n]})\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, p_k(B)(B-A)p_k(A), K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[ \Gamma_B(f^{[n-1]})\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, p_k(B)p_k(A) K_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1})\\
& \ \ \ \ - \left[ \Gamma_A(f^{[n-1]})\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-2}, p_k(B)p_k(A)K_{j-1}, K_j \ldots, K_{n-1}).
\end{split}
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Left-hand side converges, giving (24).

nodes.name: Remove cut-offs
nodes.statement: Finally, note that $(p_k(B))_{k\geq 1}$ and $(p_k(A))_{k\geq 1}$ converge strongly to the identity as $k$ goes to $\infty$ so $p_k(B)p_k(A) K_j \to K_j$ and $p_k(B)p_k(A)K_{j-1} \to K_{j-1}$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, as $k$ goes to $\infty$. By assumption, $B-A \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ so we have $p_k(B)(B-A)p_k(A) \to B-A$ as $k$ goes to $\infty$. Hence, taking the limit on $k$ in \eqref{eqfunc4} concludes the proof in the case when $2 \leq j \leq n-1$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Let $k\to\infty$ to conclude for $2\le j\le n-1$.

nodes.name: Cases j=1 and j=n
nodes.statement_short: The cases $j=1$ and $j=n$ are analogous.

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: In this proof, we will use the notation introduced before the statement of Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. For any $k\geq 1$, we let $\psi_k := \varphi_{n,g_k}$ to be the function defined as in the proof of Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. For any bounded Borel function $g$, we let $\tilde{g}$ to be the function defined on $\mathbb{R}$ by $\tilde{g}_k(x) = g(x, \ldots, x), x\in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the approximants $\psi_k=\varphi_{n,g_k}$ and diagonal restriction $\tilde g$.

nodes.name: Claim for approximants
nodes.statement:
Let us prove first that for any $k\geq 1$,
$$
\left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) = \tilde{\psi}_k(A)Z_1\ldots Z_n.
$$
Fix $k\geq 1$. $A$ is bounded so $\sigma(A) \subset \mathbb{R}$ is bounded and by definition,
$$\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k) = \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\phi_k)$$
where $\phi_k$ is the class in $L^{\infty}(\lambda_A \times \cdots \times \lambda_A)$ of the restriction of $\psi_k$ to $\sigma(A)^{n+1}$. $g_k$ is continuous on the compact $I= \text{conv}(\sigma(A))$ so there exists a sequence $(P^k_j)_{j\geq 1}$ of polynomial functions converging uniformly to $g_k$ on $I$. For any $j\geq 1$, define $Q^k_j = \varphi_{n, P^k_j}$. It is easy to see that $(Q^k_j)_{j\geq 1}$ converges uniformly to $\psi_k$ on $\sigma(A)^{n+1}$. According to \eqref{DDint}, $Q^k_j = (R^k_j)^{[n]}$ where $R^k_j$ is a polynomial function on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $(R^k_j)^{(n)} = P^k_j$. Hence $Q^k_j$ is a $(n+1)$-variable polynomial function, and in particular, $Q^k_j \in \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \cdots \otimes \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R})$. Note that for an elementary tensor $g = g_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes g_{n+1} \in \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \cdots \otimes \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R})$, we have
\begin{align*}
\left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(g) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)
& = g_1(A)Z_1g_2(A)\ldots g_n(A)Z_ng_{n+1}(A) \\
& = g_1(A)\ldots g_{n+1}(A) Z_1 \ldots Z_n \\
& = \tilde{g}(A) Z_1 \ldots Z_n.
\end{align*}
By linearity, this implies that for any $j \geq 1$,
\begin{equation} \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(Q^k_j) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) = \tilde{Q}^k_j(A)Z_1\ldots Z_n.
\end{equation}
For any $j\geq 1$, we let $v^k_j \in \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R})$ be such that $v^k_j = P^k_j$ on $I$ and  $v^k_j \to g_k$ uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$. Then
$$
\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\varphi_{n, P^k_j}) = \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\varphi_{n, v^k_j})
$$
and by Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$, there exists a constant $c_{p,n}$ such that
\begin{align*}
& \| \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(Q^k_j) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) - \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) \|_p \\
& = \| \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\varphi_{n, v^k_j} - \varphi_{n, g_k}) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) \|_p \\
& \leq c_{p,n} \| v^k_j - g_k\|_{\infty} \|Z_1\|_p \cdots \|Z_n\|_p \\
& \underset{j\to \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0.
\end{align*}
Note that $(\tilde{Q}^k_j)_{j\geq 1}$ converges uniformly to $\tilde{\phi}_k$ on $\sigma(A)$. Hence, $\tilde{Q}^k_j(A)$ converges to $\tilde{\psi}_k(A)$ in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ so that the right-hand side of \eqref{eqcomm0} converges in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ to $\tilde{\psi}_k(A)Z_1\ldots Z_n$. By taking the limit on $j$ in \eqref{eqcomm0} we get
\begin{equation} \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) = \tilde{\psi}_k(A)Z_1\ldots Z_n.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $\Gamma^{A,\dots,A}(\psi_k)(Z)=\tilde\psi_k(A)Z_1\cdots Z_n$.

nodes.name: Restrict to the spectrum
nodes.statement:
Fix $k\geq 1$. $A$ is bounded so $\sigma(A) \subset \mathbb{R}$ is bounded and by definition,
$$\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k) = \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\phi_k)$$
where $\phi_k$ is the class in $L^{\infty}(\lambda_A \times \cdots \times \lambda_A)$ of the restriction of $\psi_k$ to $\sigma(A)^{n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $A$ is bounded, only values on $\sigma(A)^{n+1}$ matter.

nodes.name: Polynomial approximation
nodes.statement: $g_k$ is continuous on the compact $I= \text{conv}(\sigma(A))$ so there exists a sequence $(P^k_j)_{j\geq 1}$ of polynomial functions converging uniformly to $g_k$ on $I$. For any $j\geq 1$, define $Q^k_j = \varphi_{n, P^k_j}$. It is easy to see that $(Q^k_j)_{j\geq 1}$ converges uniformly to $\psi_k$ on $\sigma(A)^{n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $g_k$ uniformly by polynomials $P^k_j$ and set $Q^k_j=\varphi_{n,P^k_j}$.

nodes.name: Q is polynomial
nodes.statement: According to \eqref{DDint}, $Q^k_j = (R^k_j)^{[n]}$ where $R^k_j$ is a polynomial function on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $(R^k_j)^{(n)} = P^k_j$. Hence $Q^k_j$ is a $(n+1)$-variable polynomial function, and in particular, $Q^k_j \in \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \cdots \otimes \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R})$.
nodes.statement_short: By (15), $Q^k_j$ is a divided difference of a polynomial, hence a polynomial.

nodes.name: Commuting tensors
nodes.statement_short: On elementary tensors commutation gives $\tilde g(A)Z_1\cdots Z_n$, so (30).

nodes.name: Error via Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement:
For any $j\geq 1$, we let $v^k_j \in \text{Bor}(\mathbb{R})$ be such that $v^k_j = P^k_j$ on $I$ and  $v^k_j \to g_k$ uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$. Then
$$
\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\varphi_{n, P^k_j}) = \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\varphi_{n, v^k_j})
$$
and by Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$, there exists a constant $c_{p,n}$ such that
\begin{align*}
& \| \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(Q^k_j) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) - \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) \|_p \\
& = \| \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\varphi_{n, v^k_j} - \varphi_{n, g_k}) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) \|_p \\
& \leq c_{p,n} \| v^k_j - g_k\|_{\infty} \|Z_1\|_p \cdots \|Z_n\|_p \\
& \underset{j\to \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2.7 bounds the difference between $Q^k_j$ and $\psi_k$ MOIs.

nodes.name: Limit in j
nodes.statement_short: Take $j\to\infty$ to obtain (31).

nodes.name: Weak convergence by Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement:
Recall that, from the proof of Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$, the sequence $(\psi_k)_{k\geq 1}$ $w^*$-converges to $f^{[n]}$ for the $w^*$-topology of $L^{\infty}(\lambda_A \times \cdots \times \lambda_A)$ and that $(\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k))_{k\geq 1} \subset \mathcal{B}_n(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))$ is bounded. Hence, by Lemma $\ref{LemmeUB}$,
$$
\left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(\psi_k) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) \underset{k \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right] (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)
$$
weakly in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.3 the MOIs of $\psi_k$ converge weakly to that of $f^{[n]}$.

nodes.name: Limit in k
nodes.statement: On the other hand, $(\tilde{\psi}_k)_{k\geq 1}$ is bounded and is pointwise convergent to $\tilde{f}^{[n]}=\dfrac{1}{n!}f^{(n)}$ so $(\tilde{\psi}_k(A))_{k\geq 1}$ converges strongly to $\dfrac{1}{n!} f^{(n)}(A)$ (see e.g. the proof of \cite[Proposition 3.1]{CLSS}). This implies that the right-hand side of \eqref{eqcomm} converges in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ to $\dfrac{1}{n!} f^{(n)}(A)Z_1\ldots Z_n.$ We conclude the proof by taking the limit on $k$ in \eqref{eqcomm}, in the weak topology of $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal values converge to $f^{(n)}/n!$; take $k\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Telescoping decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Write $\psi(t)-\psi(0)$ as a telescoping sum over slots.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2.8
nodes.statement_short: Each difference is given by Proposition 2.8, yielding (32).

nodes.name: Continuity at 0
nodes.statement:
For the continuity of $\psi$ in $0$, note that by Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$ there exists a constant $c_{p,n} > 0$ such that
\begin{align*}
& \| \psi(t) - \psi(0) \|_p \\
& \leq |t| \sum_{k=1}^{j} \| \left[ \Gamma^{(A+tK)^{j-k+1},(A)^{n-j+k}}(f^{[n]}) \right](X_1, \ldots, X_{j-k}, K, X_{j-k+1}, \ldots, X_{n-1}) \|_p \\
& \leq |t| j c_{p,n} \|f^{(n)} \|_{\infty} \|K\|_p \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \| X_i \|_p,
\end{align*}
which converges to $0$ as $t$ goes to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2.7 bounds the right-hand side by $O(|t|)$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement:
Let $K\in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ selfadjoint and show that $\psi$ is differentiable in $0$ with
$$
\psi'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
$$
nodes.statement_short: State the goal for arbitrary selfadjoint $K$.

nodes.name: Approximate K by K_0
nodes.statement:
Let $\epsilon > 0$ and choose $K_0 \in X_0$ such that $\|K-K_0\|_p \leq \epsilon$. By assumption, $\psi_0$ is differentiable in $0$ and
$$
\psi_0'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_0, \ldots, K_0).
$$
Hence, there exists $\mu > 0$ such that for any $|t| < \mu$,
\begin{equation} \|\psi_0(t) - \psi_0(0) - n t \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_0, \ldots, K_0) \|_p \leq |t| \epsilon.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pick $K_0$ in the dense set within $\epsilon$ and use its differentiability, (33).

nodes.name: Mixed function via Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement:
Define $\tilde{\psi} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ by
$$
\tilde{\psi}(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK_0, \ldots A+tK_0}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K), t\in \mathbb{R}.
$$
By Lemma $\ref{simplification5}$ we have
\begin{align*}
\tilde{\psi}(t) - \tilde{\psi}(0)
& = t \sum_{k=1}^n \left[ \Gamma^{(A+tK_0)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right]((K)^{n-k}, K_0, (K)^{k-1}) \\
& = t \sum_{k=1}^n \left[ \Gamma^{(A+tK_0)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_0, \ldots, K_0) + t\psi_{\epsilon}(t) \\
& = \psi_0(t) - \psi_0(0) + t\psi_{\epsilon}(t)
\end{align*}
where
$$
\psi_{\epsilon}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \Gamma_{A,K_0,k,t}((K)^{n-k}, K_0, (K)^{k-1}) - \Gamma_{A,K_0,k,t}(K_0,\ldots,K_0) \right).
$$
with $\Gamma_{A,K_0,k,t} = \Gamma^{(A+tK_0)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]})$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\tilde\psi$ and expand it with Lemma 3.6.

nodes.name: Estimate for tilde psi
nodes.statement:
By Remark $\ref{Ineqmulti}$ and Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$, there exists a constant $\alpha > 0$ depending only on $p, n, \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}$ and $\|K\|_p$ such that for any $1 \leq k \leq n$ and any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, 
$$
\| \Gamma_{A,K_0,k,t}((K)^{n-k}, K_0, (K)^{k-1}) - \Gamma_{A,K_0,k,t}(K_0, \ldots, K_0) \|_p \leq \alpha \epsilon
$$
so that we have the estimate $\| \psi_{\epsilon}(t) \| \leq n \alpha \epsilon.$ By the estimate \eqref{psiepsilon0} and triangle inequality, we deduce that for any $|t| < \mu$,
\begin{align} \begin{split}
& \| \tilde{\psi}(t) - \tilde{\psi}(0) - n t \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_0, \ldots, K_0) \|_p \\
& \leq \| \psi_0(t) - \psi_0(0)  - n t \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_0, \ldots, K_0) \|_p + |t| \| \psi_{\epsilon}(t) \|_p \\
& \leq |t| \epsilon (n\alpha + 1).
\end{split}
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\psi_\epsilon$ and get (34).

nodes.name: Estimate psi - tilde psi
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.6 again gives (35).

nodes.name: Estimate at A
nodes.statement_short: Bound the change of $\Gamma^{A,\dots,A}(f^{[n]})$ from $K$ to $K_0$, (36).

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement:
Finally, by triangle inequality and noting that $\psi(0) = \tilde{\psi}(0)$ we have, by \eqref{psiepsilon2}, \eqref{psiepsilon4} and \eqref{psiepsilon3}, 
\begin{align*}
& \| \psi(t) - \psi(0) - n t \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) \|_p \\
& \leq \| \psi(t) - \tilde{\psi}(t)\|_p \\
& \ \ \ \ + \| \tilde{\psi}(t) - \tilde{\psi}(0) - n t \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_0, \ldots, K_0)\|_p \\
& \ \ \ \ + \| n t \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_0, \ldots, K_0) - nt \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) \|_p \\
& \leq |t| \epsilon (n\beta + n\alpha + n\gamma  + 1),
\end{align*}
for any $|t| < \mu$. This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality yields differentiability at 0.

nodes.name: Differentiability of tilde psi
nodes.statement_short: Use differentiability of $\tilde\psi$ at 0, (37).

nodes.name: Path close to the line
nodes.statement_short: $((A+tK)-\nu(t))/t$ is small in $\mathcal{S}^p$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2.8
nodes.statement_short: Express $(\psi-\tilde\psi)/t$ by Proposition 2.8 and bound it, (38).

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement:
Finally, by \eqref{nu1} and \eqref{nu2} and by triangle inequality we have, noting that $\psi(0) = \tilde{\psi}(0)$,
\begin{align*}
\| \psi(t) - \psi(0) - t \tilde{\psi}'(0) \|_p
& \leq \| \psi(t) -  \tilde{\psi}(t)\|_p + \| \tilde{\psi}(t) - \tilde{\psi}(0) - t \tilde{\psi}'(0) \|_p \\
& \leq (n\alpha + 1) |t| \epsilon,
\end{align*}
for any $|t| < \text{min}(\mu_1, \mu_2)$, which proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality gives the claim.

nodes.name: Case Y in S^2: commutation
nodes.statement:
We first assume that $Y\in \mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{H})$. Note that the projection $E_m$ commutes with $A + K_m$ so that for any $g\in C_b(\mathbb{R})$ we have, by \cite[(7.25)]{KPSS},
$$
E_m g(A + K_m) = g(A_m + K_m) = g(A + K_m) E_m .
$$
nodes.statement_short: For $Y\in\mathcal{S}^2$, $E_m$ commutes with $A+K_m$ and intertwines functional calculi.

nodes.name: Tensor symbols
nodes.statement:
From this equality, we easily deduce that for any $\phi \in C_b(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \cdots \otimes C_b(\mathbb{R})$,
\begin{equation} \left[\Gamma^{A+K_m, \ldots, A+K_m}(\phi) \right](Y_m, \ldots, Y_m) 
= \left[\Gamma^{A_m+K_m, \ldots, A_m+K_m}(\phi) \right](Y_m, \ldots, Y_m).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Deduce (40) for tensor products of $C_b$ functions.

nodes.name: Uniform closure
nodes.statement: By approximation, this implies that \eqref{reducbddeq2} holds true whenever $\phi$ belongs to the uniform closure of $C_b(\mathbb{R})\otimes \cdots \otimes  C_b(\mathbb{R})$, which contains in particular $C_0(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to the uniform closure, including $C_0(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$.

nodes.name: Symbols in C_b
nodes.statement:
Assume now that $\phi \in C_b(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$. Let
$(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ be a sequence of functions in
$C_0(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying the following two properties:
$$
\forall\, k\in\mbox{${\mathbb N}$}, \quad 0\leq g_k\leq 1,
\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\forall\, r\in \mathbb{R},\quad
g_k(r)\overset{k\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1.
$$
nodes.statement_short: For $\phi\in C_b$, introduce cut-offs $g_k$.

nodes.name: Apply to phi g_k
nodes.statement:
For any $k\geq 1, \phi g_k \in C_0(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$, so the latter implies that
\begin{equation} \left[\Gamma^{A+K_m, \ldots, A+K_m}(\phi g_k) \right](Y_m, \ldots, Y_m) 
= \left[\Gamma^{A_m+K_m, \ldots, A_m+K_m}(\phi g_k) \right](Y_m, \ldots, Y_m).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The $C_0$ case gives (41).

nodes.name: Weak-* limit
nodes.statement:
By Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem, the properties satisfied by the sequence $(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ imply that $(\phi g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ converges to $\phi$ for the $w^*$-topology of $L^{\infty}\left(\prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{A + K_m}\right)$ and $L^{\infty}\left(\prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{A_m + K_m}\right)$. Hence, by the $w^*$-continuity of multiple operator integrals, we obtain, by taking the limit on $k$ in \eqref{reducbddeq1},
\begin{equation} \left[\Gamma^{A+K_m, \ldots, A+K_m}(\phi) \right](Y_m, \ldots, Y_m) 
= \left[\Gamma^{A_m+K_m, \ldots, A_m+K_m}(\phi) \right](Y_m, \ldots, Y_m).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $w^*$-continuity gives (42) for $\phi$.

nodes.name: Pass to f^[n]
nodes.statement: For any $k\geq 1$, let $\phi_k = \varphi_{n,g_k}$ as defined in the proof of Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. Then $(\varphi_{n,g_k})_{k\geq 1} \subset C_b(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ and the sequence $w^*$-converges to $f^{[n]}$ for the $w^*$-topologies of $L^{\infty}\left(\prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{A + K_m}\right)$ and $L^{\infty}\left(\prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{A_m + K_m}\right)$. Hence, $\phi_k$ satisfies \eqref{reducbddeq3} for any $k\geq 1$ and by the $w^*$-continuity of multiple operator integrals, we get that $\phi$ satisfies \eqref{reducbddeq}.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $f^{[n]}$ by $\varphi_{n,g_k}$ and conclude (39).

nodes.name: General p
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $Y$ in $\mathcal{S}^p$ using Theorem 2.7.

nodes.name: Base case n=1
nodes.statement:
The assumptions on $f$ ensure, by \cite[Theorem 7.13]{KPSS}, that $\varphi$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and that for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\varphi'(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(f^{[1]}) \right](K).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Base case from [KPSS, Theorem 7.13].

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Assume now that $\varphi$ is $(n-1)$-times differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ with
$$
\dfrac{\varphi^{(n-1)}(t)}{(n-1)!} = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Assume the formula for $\varphi^{(n-1)}$.

nodes.name: Reduction to psi
nodes.statement:
We have to show that the function
$$
\psi : t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K)
$$
is differentiable and that for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\psi'(t) = n \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
$$
It is clear that we only have to prove the differentiability in $0$, from which we can deduce the differentiabily on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that $\psi$ is differentiable with the expected derivative, and only at $0$.

nodes.name: Reduction to a dense set
nodes.statement: In this case, by Lemma $\ref{simplification3}$, it is sufficient to prove the differentiability for $K$ belonging to a dense subset of $(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.7 it suffices to treat $K$ in a dense subset.

nodes.name: Dense set i[A,Y]+Z
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Proposition 6.2]{KPSS}, the subspace $X_0$ defined by
$$
X_0 = \left\lbrace i[A,Y] + Z \ \text{with} \ Y,Z \in (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}} \ \text{and} \ Z \ \text{commutes with} \ A \right\rbrace \subset (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}
$$
is dense in $(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}$.
nodes.statement_short: [KPSS] gives density of $X_0=\{i[A,Y]+Z\}$.

nodes.name: Goal for K in X_0
nodes.statement:
Let $K = i[A,Y] + Z \in X_0$ and show that
$$
\psi_0 : t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K)
$$
is differentiable in $0$ with
$$
\psi_0'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Fix $K=i[A,Y]+Z$ and state the goal for $\psi_0$.

nodes.name: Change of path via Lemma 3.8
nodes.statement:
Let $\nu(t) = e^{-itY}(A+tZ)e^{itY}$. We have $\nu(0)=A$ and $\nu$ is $\mathcal{S}^p$-differentiable in $0$ with $\nu'(0)=K$. Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification4}$, to prove the latter, it is equivalent to prove that $\tilde{\psi} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ defined by
$$
\tilde{\psi}(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{\nu(t),\ldots,\nu(t)}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K), t\in \mathbb{R},
$$
is differentiable in $0$ with
$$
\tilde{\psi}'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Use the path $\nu(t)$ and Lemma 3.8 to reduce to $\tilde\psi$.

nodes.name: Difference quotient via Prop. 2.8
nodes.statement_short: Express the difference quotient of $\tilde\psi$ via Proposition 2.8.

nodes.name: Replace (nu(t)-A)/t by K
nodes.statement:
For $1\leq k\leq n$ and any $t
eq 0$, let
$$\displaystyle \Gamma_{
u,k}(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{(
u(t))^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})ight]\left( (K)^{n-k},  rac{
u(t) - A}{t} , (K)^{k-1} ight).$$
Since $ rac{
u(t) - A}{t}$ goes to $K$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$, by uniform boundedness of $\Gamma^{(
u(t))^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \in \mathcal{B}_n(\mathcal{S}^p), t\in \mathbb{R}$, we deduce that if one of those limits exists, so does the second one and we have
$$
\underset{t 	o 0}{\lim} \ \Gamma_{
u,k}(t) = \underset{t 	o 0}{\lim} \ \left[ \Gamma^{(
u(t))^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})ight]\left( K,\ldots,K ight).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Uniform boundedness allows replacing $(\nu(t)-A)/t$ by $K$ in the limit.

nodes.name: Unitary conjugation identity
nodes.statement_short: Unitary conjugation moves $e^{\pm itY}$ out of the MOI.

nodes.name: General conjugation identity
nodes.statement_short: Prove the conjugation identity for all symbols by tensors, $w^*$-continuity and density.

nodes.name: Remove the unitaries
nodes.statement_short: As $t\to0$ the unitaries tend to $1$, so only $\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]})(K,\dots,K)$ matters.

nodes.name: Reduce to the limit of xi
nodes.statement:
Define
$$
\xi(t) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^n \left[ \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})\right] (K, \ldots, K), t \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
The latter implies that if $\xi$ has a limit in $0$, then so does $\dfrac{\tilde{\psi}(t) - \tilde{\psi}(0)}{t}$ with the same limit. Hence, in order to prove Formula \eqref{diffenrential}, we have to show that $\xi$ has a limit in $0$ and that
$$
\underset{t \to 0}{\lim} \ \xi(t) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) \ \ \text{in} \ \ \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}).
$$
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show $\xi(t)\to n\Gamma^{A,\dots,A}(f^{[n]})(K,\dots,K)$.

nodes.name: Expand K = i[A,Y]+Z
nodes.statement:
For any $1\leq k\leq n$ and any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, let $\Gamma_k(t) = \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]}).$
Since $K = i[A,Y] + Z$, we have, for any $1\leq k \leq n$,
\begin{align*}
\left[\Gamma_k(t) \right](K,\ldots,K)
&  = \left[ \Gamma_k(t) \right] (Z, \ldots, Z) \\
&  + \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \\\text{or} \ K_m=Z, \\ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma_k(t) \right] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand each term multilinearly in $Z$ and $i[A,Y]$.

nodes.name: Expansion of xi
nodes.statement_short: Sum the expansions to write $\xi(t)$.

nodes.name: Commuting part
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 3.6 and 3.5 turn the $Z$-terms into a difference quotient of $f^{(n-1)}$.

nodes.name: Kissin-Shulman limit
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Lemma 3.4 (ii)]{KS}, this quantity converges as $t$ goes to $0$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ to
$$
\dfrac{1}{(n-1)!} \ f^{(n)}(A) Z^n.
$$
nodes.statement_short: By [KS] this converges to $f^{(n)}(A)Z^n/(n-1)!$.

nodes.name: Back to MOI
nodes.statement:
Since $n! f^{[n]}(x,\ldots,x) = f^{(n)}(x)$, the latter is in turn, by Lemma $\ref{MOIcomm}$, equal to
$$
n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](Z, \ldots, Z).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.5 rewrites the limit as $n\Gamma^{A,\dots,A}(f^{[n]})(Z,\dots,Z)$.

nodes.name: Commutator terms converge
nodes.statement:
We will now show that for any $1\leq j,k \leq n$ and for any $K_1, \ldots, K_{n-1}$ with $K_m= Z$ or $i[A,Z]$, $1\leq m \leq n-1$, 
$$
\left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})
$$
goes to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$.

Assume first that $n-k+2 \leq j \leq n$. Since $A$ and $Z$ are bounded operators, we have, by Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$,
\begin{align*}
& \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}),
\end{align*}
with a simple modification in the case $j=n$. By Lemma $\ref{simplification5}$ the latter converges, as $t$ goes to $0$, to
\begin{align*}
&\left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& - \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}),
\end{align*}
which is in turn equal to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$.

Assume now that $j=n-k+1$. In this case, by Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$,
\begin{align*}
& \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, (A+tZ)Y - YA, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}).
\end{align*}
Since $(A+tZ)Y - YA = [A,Y] +tZY$, we get
\begin{align*}
& \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}).
\end{align*}
The inequality
\begin{align*}
& \| t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \|_p \\
& \leq |t| c_{p,n} \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty} \|K_1\|_p \ldots \|K_{n-1}\|_p \|ZY\|_p
\end{align*}
and the same reasoning as for the case $n-k+2 \leq j \leq n$ show that
$$
\left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})
$$
converges to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$.

Finally, assume that $1\leq j \leq n-k$. By Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$,
\begin{align*}
& \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A+tZ,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}),
\end{align*}
with a simple modification in the case $j=1$ as in Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$. Note that $[A+tZ,Y] = [A,Y] + t[Z,Y]$ and then reason as in the previous case to show that
$$
\left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})
$$
goes to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: each commutator term converges to its value at $t=0$.

nodes.name: Case n-k+2<=j<=n
nodes.statement_short: Remark 2.9 and Lemma 3.6 give convergence.

nodes.name: Case j=n-k+1
nodes.statement:
Assume now that $j=n-k+1$. In this case, by Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$,
\begin{align*}
& \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, (A+tZ)Y - YA, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}).
\end{align*}
Since $(A+tZ)Y - YA = [A,Y] +tZY$, we get
\begin{align*}
& \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}).
\end{align*}
The inequality
\begin{align*}
& \| t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \|_p \\
& \leq |t| c_{p,n} \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty} \|K_1\|_p \ldots \|K_{n-1}\|_p \|ZY\|_p
\end{align*}
and the same reasoning as for the case $n-k+2 \leq j \leq n$ show that
$$
\left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})
$$
converges to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Remark 2.9 with an $O(t)$ correction term.

nodes.name: Case j<=n-k
nodes.statement:
Finally, assume that $1\leq j \leq n-k$. By Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$,
\begin{align*}
& \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A+tZ,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}),
\end{align*}
with a simple modification in the case $j=1$ as in Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$. Note that $[A+tZ,Y] = [A,Y] + t[Z,Y]$ and then reason as in the previous case to show that
$$
\left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})
$$
goes to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Same reasoning with $[A+tZ,Y]=[A,Y]+t[Z,Y]$.

nodes.name: Limit of xi
nodes.statement:
Hence, we proved that
\begin{align*}
& \underset{t \to 0}{\lim} \ \xi(t) \\
& = n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](Z, \ldots, Z) \\
& \ \ \ \ + \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \\\text{or} \ K_m=Z, \\ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\
& = n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
\end{align*}
This proves that $\varphi \in D^n(\mathbb{R},{\mathcal{S}}^p(\mbox{${\mathcal H}$}))$ and that for any $1\leq k \leq n$, $\varphi^{(k)}$ is given by \eqref{diffenrential}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine: $\xi(t)\to n\Gamma^{A,\dots,A}(f^{[n]})(K,\dots,K)$, proving the formula.

nodes.name: Local boundedness setup
nodes.statement_short: On a bounded interval replace $f$ by a compactly supported $C^i$ function $f_i$.

nodes.name: Boundedness of derivatives
nodes.statement: Hence, since $f_i^{(i)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi^{(i)}$ is bounded on $I$ by Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. Similarly, since $f^{(n)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi^{(n)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2.7 bounds $\varphi^{(i)}$ on $I$ and $\varphi^{(n)}$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: By \cite[Theorem 7.18]{KPSS}, $\varphi$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi'(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(f^{[1]}) \right](K).$
nodes.statement_short: Base case from [KPSS, Theorem 7.18].

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Assume now that $\varphi$ is $(n-1)$-times differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ with
$$
\dfrac{\varphi^{(n-1)}(t)}{(n-1)!} = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Assume the formula for $\varphi^{(n-1)}$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement:
We will prove that the function
$$
\psi : t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K)
$$
is differentiable in $0$ and that
\begin{equation} \psi'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Show $\psi$ is differentiable at $0$ with derivative (43).

nodes.name: Dense set of compressions
nodes.statement:
For any $m\geq 1$, let $E_m = \chi_{[-m,m]}(A)$. Then $A_m := AE_m$ is bounded. Note that $(E_m)_{m\geq 1}$ converges strongly to the identity so for any $K\in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, $K_m:=E_m K E_m$ converges to $K$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $m$ goes to $\infty$. This implies that the set
$$
X_0 = \left\lbrace K_m \ | \ K \in (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}, m\geq 1 \right\rbrace \subset (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}
$$
is dense in $(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}$. Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification3}$, we only have to prove \eqref{unbbproof} for $K$ element of $X_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compressions $K_m=E_mKE_m$ are dense, so by Lemma 3.7 it suffices to treat them.

nodes.name: Reduce to bounded A_m
nodes.statement:
Let $K=K_m \in X_0$ for some $m\geq 1$.
By Lemma $\ref{reducbdd}$, we have, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\psi(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A_m+tK_m, \ldots, A_m+tK_m}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m)
$$
which is, by Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$, differentiable in $0$ with
$$
\psi'(0) = n\left[\Gamma^{A_m, \ldots, A_m}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.9 and Theorem 3.1 give differentiability via the bounded $A_m$.

nodes.name: Back to A
nodes.statement:
Using Lemma $\ref{reducbdd}$ again, we see that
$$
\psi'(0) = n\left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m).
$$
This proves that $\varphi \in D^n(\mathbb{R},{\mathcal{S}}^p(\mbox{${\mathcal H}$}))$ and that the derivatives of $\varphi$ are given by \eqref{diffenrentialunbdd}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.9 again identifies the derivative.

nodes.name: Bounded derivatives
nodes.statement: Finally, the boundedness of the derivatives follows from Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness from Theorem 2.7.

nodes.name: Existence of derivatives
nodes.statement: The existence of the derivatives $\displaystyle \frac{d^k}{dt^k}\Big(f(A+tK)\Big)\Big|_{t=0}, k=1, \ldots, n-1,$ are ensured by Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$ and Theorem $\ref{FormulaSAunbdd}$.
nodes.statement_short: Derivatives exist by Theorems 3.1 and 3.2.

nodes.name: Representation by induction
nodes.statement: The representation \eqref{Taylor} can be obtained by induction on $n$, using Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. See the proof of \cite[Theorem 4.1 (ii)]{CLSS} for more details.
nodes.statement_short: Representation by induction on $n$ using Theorem 2.7, as in [CLSS].

nodes.name: Estimate
nodes.statement: From this representation, we obtain the estimate \eqref{Taylorineq} by applying Inequality \eqref{IneqDDn}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply (16) to obtain the estimate.

nodes.name: Existence via Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 gives the $n$-th derivative formula.

nodes.name: Reduce to continuity at 0
nodes.statement:
Hence, to prove the result, we have to show that the mapping
$$
t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (K, \ldots, K) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})
$$
is continuous. More generally, we will prove that for any $X = (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^n$, the mapping
$$
\varphi_X : t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})
$$
is continuous. Note that it is sufficient to prove that $\varphi_X$ is continuous in $0$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show $\varphi_X$ is continuous at $0$ for all $X$.

nodes.name: Case f^(n) in C_0
nodes.statement:
Let $h \in C^n(\mathbb{R})$.  Assume that either $A$ is bounded or $h^{(i)}$ is bounded for all $1\leq i\leq n-1$ and further assume that $h^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$. It follows from \cite[Theorem 3.4]{LMS} that $h$ is $n$-times continuously Fr\'echet $\mathcal{S}^p$-differentiable at $A$. This implies that for any $X_1, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, the mapping
\begin{equation} t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(h^{[n]}) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n)
\end{equation}
is continuous in $0$. Hence, if $f^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, $\varphi \in C^n(\mathbb{R},{\mathcal{S}}^p(\mbox{${\mathcal H}$}))$. The rest of the proof consists in reducing to this particular case.\\
nodes.statement_short: If $h^{(n)}\in C_0$, continuity follows from [LMS, Theorem 3.4]; reduce to this case.

nodes.name: Cut-off functions
nodes.statement:
Let $(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ be a sequence of $C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying the following two properties:
$$
\forall\, k\in\mbox{${\mathbb N}$}, \quad 0\leq g_k\leq 1,
\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\forall\, r\in \mathbb{R},\quad
g_k(r)\overset{k\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1.
$$
Let $k\geq 1$. Define $G_k^n = g_k \otimes \underbrace{1 \otimes \cdots \otimes 1}_{n-1 \ \text{times}} \otimes g_k$ and write
$$
G_k^n(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = h_1(x_1,x_2) h_2(x_{n-1},x_n)
$$
where $h_1 = g_k \otimes 1$ and $h_2 = 1 \otimes g_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce cut-offs $g_k$ and $G_k^n=g_k\otimes1\otimes\cdots\otimes g_k$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.4 for cut-off
nodes.statement:
We have
$$
\left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(h_1)\right](X_1) = g_k(A+tK) X_1
$$
and
$$\left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(h_2)\right](X_n) = X_n g_k(A+tK).
$$
Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$, the function
$$
\varphi_{k,X}^n : t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}G_k^n) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})
$$
satisfies, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\varphi_{k,X}^n(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right](g_k(A+tK) X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n g_k(A+tK)).
$$
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.4, $\varphi^n_{k,X}$ is $\varphi_X$ with cut-off arguments.

nodes.name: Cut-offs converge
nodes.statement: $(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ is bounded and pointwise convergent to $1$ so $(g_k(A))_{k\geq 1}$ converges strongly to the identity of $\mathcal{H}$ and hence $g_k(A) X_1 \to X_1$ and $X_n g_k(A) \to X_n$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $k\to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $g_k(A)\to I$ strongly, so cut-off arguments converge.

nodes.name: Resolvent strong convergence
nodes.statement:
Moreover, it follows from the arguments of the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.4]{CLSS} that $A + tK \to A$ resolvent strongly as $t \to 0$. This means that for any $u \in C_b(\mathbb{R})$,
$$
u(A+tK) \underset{t \to 0}{\longrightarrow} u(A) \ \ \text{strongly}.
$$
For any $k\geq 1, g_k \in C_b(\mathbb{R})$ so $g_k(A+tK) \to g_k(A)$ strongly as $t \to 0$, which implies that $g_k(A+tK) X_1 \to g_k(A) X_1$ and $X_n g_k(A+tK) \to X_n g_k(A)$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t\to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $A+tK\to A$ in the strong resolvent sense, so $g_k(A+tK)\to g_k(A)$ strongly.

nodes.name: Choose k_0 and t_0
nodes.statement:
Let $\epsilon > 0$. By the latter, there exists $k_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that, for any $k\geq k_0$,
$$
\| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A) K\|_p \leq \epsilon \ \ \text{and} \ \ \| X_n - X_n g_{k_0}(A) \|_p \leq \epsilon
$$
and there exists $t_0 > 0$ such that for any $|t| \leq t_0$,
$$
\| g_{k_0}(A)X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \leq \epsilon \ \ \text{and} \ \ \| X_n g_{k_0}(A) - X_n g_{k_0}(A+tK) \|_p \leq \epsilon.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Choose $k_0$ and $t_0$ making the cut-off errors at most $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Uniform cut-off error
nodes.statement:
Hence, for any $|t| \leq t_0$,
\begin{align*}
& \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \\
& \leq \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A) X_1\|_p + \| g_{k_0}(A)X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \\
& \leq 2 \epsilon,
\end{align*}
and similarly,
$$
\| X_n - X_n g_{k_0}(A+tK) \|_p \leq 2\epsilon.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality bounds $\|X_1-g_{k_0}(A+tK)X_1\|_p\le2\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Compare with cut-off
nodes.statement:
By Remark $\ref{Ineqmulti}$ and Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$, there exists a constant $C > 0$ depending only on $p, n, \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}$ and $\|K\|_p$ such that, for any $|t| < t_0$,
$$
\| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) \|_p \leq C \epsilon.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Remark 2.2 and Theorem 2.7 give $\|\varphi_X-\varphi^n_{k_0,X}\|_p\le C\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Reduce to cut-off functions
nodes.statement:
By the triangle inequality we get that for any $|t| < t_0$,
\begin{align*}
& \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_X(0) \|_p \\
& \leq \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) \|_p + \|\varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) \|_p + \| \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) - \varphi_X(0)\|_p \\
& \leq 2C \epsilon + \|\varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) \|_p.
\end{align*}
Hence, to prove the result, it suffices to prove that for any $k\geq 1$ and any $X \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^n, \varphi_{k,X}^n$ is continuous in $0$.\\
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove continuity of each $\varphi^n_{k,X}$ at $0$.

nodes.name: Induction set-up
nodes.statement: Fix $k\geq 1$ and let $g = g_k$. We will prove the continuity of $\varphi_{k,X}^n$ in $0$ by induction on $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove continuity of $\varphi^n_{k,X}$ by induction on $n$.

nodes.name: Base case: product formula
nodes.statement_short: For $n=1$ write $f^{[1]}g\otimes g$ via $(gf)^{[1]}$ and $g^{[1]}$ and apply Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: Base case: continuity
nodes.statement_short: Both terms are continuous at 0 by the $C_0$ case.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Now, let $n\geq 2$ and assume that for any $1\leq i \leq n-1$ and any $X=(X_1,\ldots, X_{i}) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^i$, $\varphi_{k,X}^{i}$ is continuous in $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume continuity for orders below $n$.

nodes.name: Leibniz-type formula
nodes.statement:
First, we show by induction the following formula: for every $(x_0,\ldots,x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$,
\begin{align} \begin{split}
& f^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n)g(x_0) \\
& = (gf)^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_n) g^{[n]}(x_0,\ldots, x_n) - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l]}(x_0, \ldots, x_l)f^{[n-l]}(x_{l} ,\ldots, x_n).
\end{split}
\end{align}
For $n=2$, first note that the computations made in \eqref{calculsn1} give
$$
f^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)g(x_0) = (gf)^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) - f(x_1)g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)
$$
so that
\begin{align*}
& f^{[2]}(x_0,x_1,x_2)g(x_0) \\
& = \dfrac{f^{[1]}(x_0,x_2)g(x_0) - f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} + \dfrac{f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)g(x_1) - f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)g(x_0)}{x_0-x_1} \\
& = \dfrac{(gf)^{[1]}(x_0,x_2) - f(x_2)g^{[1]}(x_0,x_2) - (gf)^{[1]}(x_1,x_2) + f(x_2)g^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)}{x_0-x_1} \\
& \ \ \ \ - g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2) \\
& = (gf)^{[2]}(x_0,x_1,x_2) - f(x_2) g^{[2]}(x_0,x_1,x_2) - g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2),
\end{align*}
which shows \eqref{recfng} for $n=2$. Assume now that we have \eqref{recfng} at the order $n$ and show that it still holds true at the order $n+1$. We have
\begin{align} \begin{split}
& f^{[n+1]}(x_0,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) \\
& = \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\
& \ \ \ \ + \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0)}{x_0-x_1} \\
& = \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\
& \ \ \ \ - g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}).
\end{split}
\end{align}
By assumption, we have
\begin{align} \begin{split}
& \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\
& = \dfrac{(gf)^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1}) - (gf)^{[n]}(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1})}{x_0-x_1} \\
& \ \ \ \ - f(x_{n+1}) \dfrac{g^{[n]}(x_0,x_2,\ldots, x_{n+1}) - g^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})}{x_0-x_1} \\
& \ \ \ \ - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \dfrac{g^{[l]}(x_0,x_2, \ldots, x_{l+1})-g^{[l]}(x_1, \ldots, x_{l+1})}{x_0-x_1}f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\
& = (gf)^{[n+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{n+1}) - f(x_{n+1}) g^{[n+1]}(x_0,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\
& \ \ \ \ - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{l+1}) f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}).
\end{split}
\end{align}
We have
\begin{align*}
& \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{l+1}) f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) + g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\
& = \sum_{j=2}^{n} g^{[j]}(x_0, \ldots, x_j) f^{[n+1-j]}(x_j ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) + g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\
& = \sum_{j=1}^{n} g^{[j]}(x_0, \ldots, x_j) f^{[n+1-j]}(x_j ,\ldots, x_{n+1}).
\end{align*}
Hence, by \eqref{recu1} and \eqref{recu2}, Formula \eqref{recfng} is proved at the order $n+1$. Note that the previous computations make sense when $x_0 \neq x_1$ and by continuity, the formula also holds true for $x_0 = x_1$.

nodes.name: Decompose via Lemmas 2.4 and 2.5
nodes.statement:
Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$. Applying the operator
$$
\left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(\cdot)\right](X_1,\ldots, X_n)
$$
to the previous equality gives, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$ and Lemma $\ref{simplificationsep}$,
\begin{align*}
\varphi_{k,X}^n(t) = \varphi_1(t) - \varphi_2(t) - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \varphi_{3,l}(t)
\end{align*}
where
$$
\varphi_1(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}((gf)^{[n]})\right](X_1,\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_ng(A+tK)),
$$
$$
\varphi_2(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(g^{[n]})\right](X_1,\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n (gf)(A+tK)),
$$
and for any $1\leq l \leq n-1$,
$$
\varphi_{3,l}(t) = \varphi_{3,l}^1(t)\varphi_{3,l}^2(t)
$$
with 
$$
\varphi_{3,l}^1(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(g^{[l]})\right](X_1,\ldots,X_{l})
$$
and
$$\varphi_{3,l}^2(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-l]})\right](X_{l+1},\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n g(A+tK)).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 2.4 and 2.5 split $\varphi^n_{k,X}$ into $\varphi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_{3,l}$.

nodes.name: phi_1, phi_2 continuous
nodes.statement: The functions $g$ and $gf$ belong to $C_b(\mathbb{R})$ so the mappings $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_ng(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ and $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_n (gf)(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ are continuous in $0$. We have $(gf)^{(n)}, g^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$ so by the continuity of the map defined in \eqref{casefnC0}, we get that $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ are continuous in $0$.
nodes.statement_short: The $C_0$ case gives continuity of $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$.

nodes.name: phi_3 continuous; conclude
nodes.statement: Now let $1 \leq l \leq n-1$. Since $g^{(l)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, $\varphi_{3,l}^1$ is continuous in $0$. We have $1 \leq n-l \leq n-1$, and by assumption, $\varphi_{k,Y}^{n-l}$ is continuous in $0$ for any $Y \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^l$. Hence, by composition with the continuous map $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_ng(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, we get that $\varphi_{3,l}^2$ is continuous in $0$, so that $\varphi_{3,l}$ also is. We hence proved that $\varphi_{k,X}$ is continuous in $0$, which concludes the proof of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: The induction hypothesis gives continuity of $\varphi_{3,l}$, concluding the proof.
